title: The Woodsman
full_review:
The subject of pedophilia is so repellent that the mere theme may be a turnoff to many moviegoers, but if you can get past that "The Woodsman" (Newmarket) is a mesmerizing, if somber, story about a convicted pedophile who, after serving his 12-year sentence, attempts to reform his life.

The unsmiling and taciturn Walter (Kevin Bacon in an extraordinary performance) takes a job in a lumberyard, and though he's totally guarded about opening up to people, he enters into a romantic relationship with a tough but understanding Vickie (Kyra Sedgwick, Bacon's real-life wife), who works there as well.

Eventually, he reveals his sordid background to her, and he asks her to leave. Though normally unflappable, she expresses her horror as soon as she's alone in her car. (She later comes back to him, and reveals that she was molested as a child by her brothers.)

Mary-Kay (Eve), another woman at work, has bad vibes about Walter and unearths his prison record, later circulating the news around the company, leading to harassment from his outraged co-workers. Meanwhile, Walter must cope with suspicious Detective Lucas (Mos Def), who hounds him; subtle and overt ostracism by his family -- a sister who refuses to see him; and a brother-in-law, Carlos (Benjamin Bratt), who's all friendly affability, but patronizingly keeps Walter at arm's length.

Worst of all, his own personal demons threaten to bring him back to his old ways. He's not helped by his apartment overlooking a schoolyard with children playing, and in one harrowing scene he follows a young girl to a city park, and almost backslides to his old ways.

The subtly played (and nonexploitative) scene is one of the film's dramatic highpoints. Suddenly face to face with a little girl, the old temptations return. Walter has barely smiled through the entire film, but now, with his would-be prey, the dark cloud hanging over him lifts and he breaks into a childlike grin. He pulls back from hurting the child, when he recognizes that she -- like himself -- has been hurt.

Throughout the film, Walter's been watching a man casing the schoolyard and recognizing the signs of a fellow pedophile. His revulsion at what he knows the man is up to adds an interesting texture to the main plot line.

First-time director Nicole Kassell's compelling drama (based on a play by Steven Fechter) provides genuine insight into the mind-set of a pedophile, without glamorizing the crime or making Bacon's character unduly sympathetic, though the occasionally stagy dialogue betrays the script's theatrical origins.

The performances are all fine, and the actress named Eve is especially good as the troublemaking co-worker. Xavier Perez Grobet's cinematography is cold and gray as befitting its grim subject.

The film concludes on an appropriately redemptive note, and a hopeful sense that perhaps Walter will be able to escape his past.
Because of rough and crude language, partial nudity, a couple of sexual situations involving adults, and overall adult thematic material, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
